newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German TV offers investors cheap entry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German TV offers investors cheap entry.

text.p: German television group ProSieben Media AG on Monday offered investors the prospect of a relatively cheap entry into Germany's hot media sector by saying new shares would cost no more than 72 marks ($41.63).

Following weeks of a high-profile media campaign modelled after the hugely successful marketing blitz of phone giant Deutsche Telekom, ProSieben said the price for its shares would be set through a bookbuilding phase at between 66 and 72 marks.

The final offer price for the 17.5 million non-voting preference shares will be set over the next two weeks and will be announced on July 5, two days before the shares begin trading on Germany's stock exchanges.
The listing is worth as much as 1.26 billion marks, but the lion's share of that will go to majority shareholder Thomas Kirch rather than to the company.
ProSieben, one of the most profitable German TV groups, hopes to cash in on the Telekom effect and is hawking the issue as the only chance to get a piece of Germany's media market.

The offer is attracting interest from foreign investors, who have few opportunities to buy into the fast-changing European TV industry apart from exceptions like France's TF1 and Canal Plus or Britain's BSkyB.
ProSieben chairman Georg Kofler, sitting beneath a banner proclaiming "Germany's First Television Share", said he expected the issue would be oversubscribed several times.

Some 750,000 private investors have called the company's hotline since April to register interest in buying shares. They will be able to subscribe to the issue from June 24 to July 3 and will have to order a minimum of 50 shares.
"With the exception of Telekom, no other listing of a German company has generated as much public interest as the ProSieben share," he said.
The stock market also seemed bullish on the issue.

"I'm surprised at how cheap it is, we had expected 68 to 78. I now expect we will get a bookbuilding price of 72 marks which I would be very pleased with and we recommend subscribing to the shares," said Pierre Drach, head of Frankfurt-based equity analysis group Independent Research.

On the unofficial grey market, a kind of futures trade in shares about to list, ProSieben stock was being offered in a range of 100-110 marks, an indication that shares could surge after its debut in official bourse trade on July 7.
But analysts were cautious about the shares at that level.
"I wouldn't necessarily recommend buying them at 100 marks," said Drach. "It could be that we would issue a sell recommendation if the shares hit that level."
Like the rest of Germany's closely-held media industry, the ProSieben offering is complicated and its future shareholding structure, the target of sharp criticism, has pros and cons for investors.
After the listing all ProSieben's preferred shares will be publicly traded, but not the ordinary shares -- the only stock with voting rights.
Kirch, with close ties to his father's film and television empire, will hold 60 percent of the ordinary stock and retail group Rewe will hold the other 40 percent.
Competitors have warned potential shareholders that Kirch could use his power to the detriment of private shareholders who will have stock but no say in the company.
But Kofler said ordinary stock would be listed before 2000 and insisted the company was independent of Kirch.
"No single shareholder, not even Thomas Kirch, can force the management or supervisory board to agree to any business deal that would hurt the company or its shareholders," he said.

Using its two TV channels -- Pro7 and Kabel1 -- the company has carried out a high-powered media campaign modelled after Deutsche Telekom's hugely successful marketing blitz that convinced some two million private investors to buy its shares.
Analysts point to Telekom's $13 billion listing last November as the catalyst that sparked growing interest among ordinarily cautious German private investors in buying shares.
Lothar Lanz, ProSieben finance chief, predicted at least half of the issue would be taken up by German investors. The rest would be sold through a private placement in the United States.
"We want to serve the retail market well," said Lanz.
The issue is being managed by a banking consortium led by BHF Bank AG, Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank AG and Salomon Brothers.
--Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150 ($ = 1.729 German Marks)
